I cannot recommend this game enough.  An absolutely fantastic Metroidvania with several extra options for play.  The classic version is a well constructed experience, complete with animated and fully voiced cut scenes, a great plot, wonderful exploration, plenty of places to poke your nose into.  The game also includes a Roguelike mode with random power-ups to see how far you can get, some extra missions, and a New Game+ so you can keep playing with your inventory and upgrades.  With my only complaint being that the keyboard entry still uses keyboard commands (so WADS move the cursor around an E presses the highlighted key rather than "e" - menuing error that desperately needs to be fixed as of 1.1.7).  If you are a fan of Metroidvanias, and I know it is a fairly robust genre, this is one you don't want to sleep on.

I'm heavily saddened to write this since I consider UnEpic to be one of the best games ever created. Ghost 1.0 just isn't at the same level or even remotely close in stature. 

There are two modes, regular metroidvania mode and roguelike mode. The unfortunate thing is the game was balanced more towards the roguelike mode and as a result the metroidvania mode suffers greatly.

You are forced into combat of varying difficulty levels while exploring the map. If you die, you lose everything on your person that you've collected which would lead one to think that maybe it's leaning towards some souls-like or roguelike mechanics but sadly upon retrieving your "essence" where you previously died, you only get back a miniscule amount of your previously collected items and lose ALL upgrades and weapons acquired. The only way to mitigate this is every time you upgrade or buy a new weapon / item, you need to walk all the way back to a save point to save your game to prevent loss. This encourages unnecessary backtracking and sometimes you'll be forced to backtrack into rooms with higher difficulty levels of unskippable locked room fights due to the alarms that you cannot avoid. This is absolutely unfun and terrible game design.

The map itself is pretty bland. A lot of the rooms and other parts of the map look the same. There's nothing dynamic in the layout either. It's basically copy and paste the rectangle room over and over.

The music is serviceable but also forgettable to me which hurts to say because I absolutely ADORED the soundtrack for UnEpic.

The controls are terrible. It uses twin stick shooter controls which has been poorly implemented. You have to release aiming simply to jump. This is absolutely ridiculous.

I don't know what happened here but I'll have to skip this for sure.

Ghost 1.0 is one of those games that slips under the radar, but really shouldn’t.

It looks simple at first, but once you start playing, the tight controls, clever level design, and satisfying progression pull you in. Combat feels good, movement is responsive, and upgrades actually matter — you feel yourself improving without the game turning into a button-mashing power fantasy.

What I appreciated most is how confident the game feels. It doesn’t overexplain, it doesn’t chase trends, and it doesn’t waste your time. Exploration is rewarding, the humor lands surprisingly well, and the soundtrack quietly supports the atmosphere instead of trying to steal the spotlight.

This isn’t a flashy AAA title, and it doesn’t need to be. It’s a well-made, focused experience with personality — the kind of game you buy on sale and end up wondering why more people aren’t talking about it.

If you enjoy solid gameplay, meaningful upgrades, and games with soul, Ghost 1.0 is absolutely worth your time.

Ghost 1.0 es uno de esos juegos que no esperas que te marquen, y sin embargo, lo hacen. Tiene acción, ritmo, exploración, combates frenéticos, secretos… Todo lo que se espera de un buen metroidvania está aquí, con una ejecución sólida y sin fisuras. Pero lo que realmente lo hace brillar es el alma que transmite, esa que solo notas en juegos hechos con cariño, amor y dedicación.

Fran lo ha vuelto a hacer. Con su sello inconfundible, ha creado una experiencia redonda: divertida, exigente, y con ese equilibrio entre humor y narrativa que tan bien sabe manejar. Como toda buena obra que va más allá de lo superficial, poco a poco su historia va soltando preguntas que no esperabas: identidad, conciencia, control… No quiero spoilear, pero a nivel narrativo es una pasada.

Los protagonistas tienen su personalidad bien definida, con diálogos irónicos que te sacan una sonrisa en el momento menos pensado. No son protagonistas al uso, pero sí que te importan, y eso en un metroidvania es más raro de lo que parece. Gracias a ellos, la historia gana profundidad sin volverse pesada, y te quedas con ganas de saber más.

La estación Nakamura es casi un personaje más. Da la sensación de estar siempre activa, con sus robots y sistemas funcionando sin parar. Además, el diseño de sus zonas refuerza esa coherencia y vida. El estilo futurista y cyberpunk está perfectamente integrado, y recorrer cada rincón se siente natural y entretenido. Nada está puesto al azar: los puzzles, las alarmas, los NPCs… todo encaja con la historia y la ambientación.

Nada que añadir sobre la banda sonora: tiene tanta personalidad que acabarás tarareándola sin darte cuenta, y eso siempre es buena señal.

El doblaje al español es oro puro, aunque, personalmente, creo que no llega a la misma altura que en Unepic o Unmetal, donde la calidad es claramente superior. Aún así, es muuuuy disfrutable.

¿El juego es perfecto? No. En ocasiones presenta picos de dificultad algo abruptos y momentos anticlimáticos, además de secretos tan crípticos que parece que el juego te esté tomando el pelo, pero nada de eso eclipsa el conjunto. Son detalles anecdóticos.

En definitiva, Ghost 1.0 no pretende reinventar el género, pero tampoco le hace falta. Su objetivo es claro: ofrecer una aventura intensa, con humor, con desafío y ese sabor indie que solo puede nacer de la pasión. Y lo consigue con creces.

Gracias, Fran, de verdad. Por seguir haciendo juegos así. Por recordarnos que aún existen desarrolladores que hacen las cosas con pasión. No puedo esperar a jugar tu próximo gran título.

Enjoyed it quite a bit, but probably a somewhat niche title. Definitely more of a sale candidate if you are not in dire need of a half-serious cyberpunk metroidvania.

[i]Ghost 1.0[/i] straddles a strange line, it wants to be something of a twinstick shooter, a metroidvania, a serious cyberpunk story, a tongue-in-check cyberpunk story and nostalgic all at the same time while also attempting to innovate here and there. Does not quite work out, honestly. The gameplay is solid, but also janky at times. When I recently got back into it and tried my hand at some of the extra challenges, I noticed this somewhat severely, as the regular storymode is comparatively forgiving there with all the upgrades to make your life easier. But then again, getting those can be an outright chore, as every room has a “hidden” loot that can be unlocked in the wildest ways. Shooting a specific spot, floating somewhere in ghost form, use a lift 3 times, kill enemies in less than 5 seconds, kill all enemies EXCEPT one specific type, kill ONLY a specific type… the list goes on. It often feels random and very much “just use a guide”. What I mean to say is, the gameplay is mostly solid, very much what you would expect, but it is also trying very hard to make you find secrets in very unintuitive ways that often feel like this has to be in it because of the genre and to keep you busy, rather than engaging you with intricately interconnected map design, secret passages and such. This is fine, considering that the setting is a space station which only allows so much variety, of which there is ultimately quite a lot. Bottom line is, I did not find this groundbreakingly awesome, but sufficiently enjoyable most of the time. What I will say is that I rather like the idea of the “ghost” that can possess most of the robots that populate the space station. In this sense we can get lots of variety, for instance by playing as the combat droid for a spell.
But let us proceed to what actually drew me in. In a trailer, we see an early section wherein Ghost explodes a robot, is called out for what the hell this was supposed to be and gleefully goes “Stealth!”. That kind of blatant, unapologetic cringey humor felt just lighthearted enough for me to interest me. And oh boy, did the game deliver on this front. It is rather interesting, for as the plot progresses, we see lots of tongue-in-cheek humor and eye rolling, only missing a laugh track. We get traditional tropes… but we also get very different tones when it comes to them. The trio is developed somewhat thoroughly and actually interesting and relevant questions of the cyberpunk genre ala [i]Ghost in the Shell[/i] come up, alongside the tropey mentioning of “[i]Blade Runner[/i] rules” or whatever. We are told stories by and of other characters only for another to interject and correct that no, this was not an epic adventure, it was just D&D night. This game is [i]nerdy as hell[/i] and just runs with it. And I gotta say, I rather enjoy it for what it is here. It does not take itself too seriously, since it is after all a kind of silly shootey game, complete with the somewhat deliberately cringe voice acting and an episodic format where you are told “Last time on [i]Ghost 1.0[/i] . . . and now the conclusion!” whenever you reload, as if watching an endlessly ongoing TV show. Yet the writers showed themselves adept enough to keep from falling into the super ironic self-awareness trap and make it into one big laughing track. Again, while not groundbreaking or genre defining, I rather enjoyed it for what it is and how deliberately it celebrates a lot of 80s and 90s geek culture whenever it is not asking somewhat profound questions. Definitely a solid, fun cyberpunk experience for me. If a bit janky, but maybe that is just part of the deal.

Playing this, I asked myself "why am I putting up with this?" on several occasions. 

Having now finished the game, I still don't have an answer.

First off, no, this is not a metroidvania. The point of a metroidvania is to explore a vast environment and [b]find and acquire new abilities[/b], most often traversal abilities, that allow you to access new areas, where you'll find more new abilities, and so on and so forth. Here, the only thing preventing you from walking straight to the final boss right from the start is not having the key. A key is not a new ability. The only thing this game has in common with metroidvanias is the (somewhat) big interconnected map. Otherwise, you have almost all your full kit right from the start, and the only additional traversal abilities you can get are fully optional, acquired with skill points instead of being discovered, and never needed for exploration - the double jump helps with tricky platforming but is never outright required and the other two (air dash and glide) I never used.

Second, like Unepic before it, this game mostly offers annoyances and calls it gameplay. You lose all your stuff upon dying, and while you can reclaim items by returning to your corpse (or never lose them in the first place by saving in classic mode), your energy cubes (i.e money) are gone. And with how expensive everything is, this is a pain. Another good example is the shortcuts : at times you can enter maintenance areas that allow you to move quickly to a previous location. These areas are full of pipes. And guess what, if they're hit by a stray shot, steam starts pouring out - which hurts you. Problem : a bunch of your upgrades are about having autonomous drones accompany you. So you have a choice then : go into the menu and disable everything (and also watch your own regular shots!) then re-enable everything twenty seconds later when you're through the area, or just hit those pipes and then wait for the steam to sloooowly recede. Either way, you're screwed.

Combat is mostly fine, but on more than one occasion the game just throws barrages of unavoidable projectiles at you - you have to either tank it, or burn through tons of regen items to go through it. As for bosses, except for the first one, they're essentially all DPS checks.

But the worst of the worst is the "souls". In nearly every room, you can make some shining motes appear throughout the room, then collect them all for a reward, ranging from just some more cubes to permanent upgrades. The thing is, the conditions for making these motes appear vary from reasonnable (walk into an out of the way corner, clear an optional alarm) to absolutely impossible to reasonnably guess (crouch for 5 full seconds without moving, go back and forth on that elevator three times, wiggle in place like an idiot, kill the enemies in a particular order, use an item but from the menu not from your shortcuts, SAVE AND QUIT THEN RELOAD, open and close the menu, disable a powerup,...). Not only are some of those conditions completely unreasonnable things to do during normal gameplay, there are just so many of them that even if you were aware of them, trying all those things in every single room in the game just to see what will make the damn things appear is just plain stupid. I do not understand how you're supposed to get them without a guide. And before you ask, no, there are no hints anywhere.
You might be tempted to ignore them. But those upgrades add up, and if you get all of the souls of a particular area, you get a very powerful upgrade on top of it. So you really want to do them.

The only interesting mechanic the game has is the ability to exit your mech as a ghost, fly around, and possess other robots. It's a very neat idea, but in practice your main bot is strictly better than absolutely everything you can possess, so you only do it when you need to solve some basic puzzle, or to soften a group from afar. Oh and your main body remains vulnerable during this, so you can't use it during combat.

Structure wise, it's very simple. You arrive to an area, where you need to get the 5 pieces of the key to the next one. Doing this will take you through the [i]entire area[/i] ; there are maybe two or three rooms in the game that are truly optional, and you never need to backtrack, except at the very beginning in the central zone (since it's the one with the locked doors to the other areas). On the way you'll accomplish another story objective. Rinse and repeat, and then you're at the end. Like I said - it's not a metroidvania. There's no exploration. It's more of a slightly open action platformer.

Then, story wise... eh. I guessed the "twist" something like 30 minutes in? It's pretty standard, you can see it coming from a mile away the moment the first element of "foreshadowing" drops. And other than the forgettable story this is "Pop culture : The Game" - to the point where the game doesn't just make references but outright namedrops some of the stuff it talks about. All of this serviced by amateur voice acting that varies between "fine, I guess" to "ugh shut up" in quality.

Anyway, I didn't like it.

Ghost 1.0 was an amazing experience for me. Different in many ways from UnEpic, the developer's previous title, but still maintaining the beautifully comedic tone that the developer is known for. I want to specifically call out how fun the character writing is, filled with cheesy and somewhat dated yet equally heartwarming comedy, and supported by the amazing voice-acting for the trio of main characters, making every dialogue just a joy to listen to. In simple words, the game is so full of heart and joy that it took me back to my earlier days, when gaming was so much simpler)

Design-wise, Ghost 1.0 is a fun mix of 2D-action with Metroidvania elements, both of which are done quite well. Unlike many metroidvanias, Ghost 1.0 doesn't throw many new abilities at you, deciding to focus more on the slow improvement of your already-existent arsenal by unraveling the secrets of the space-station that you're exploring, additionally throwing in new subweapons, many of which I did find to be quite lacking, as it is quite possible to complete the game with just a couple of bought weapons. 

One of the main staples of the genre which Ghost 1.0 handles quite well is exploration and secret-hunting — the Nakamura space-station if filled to the brink with secrets, many of which are close to impossible to unravel without the help of a guide, requiring you to perform a series of improbable actions such as save & quit the game. Funny in many ways, but not a very good design choice.

There are some other game-design issues that I've found quite annoying, but overall Ghost 1.0 offers an enjoyable gaming experience, improving on many elements of UnEpic, while moving in a slightly different direction. Still, the game's writing is one of its core strengths, as it's been a while since I've smiled so much during my playthrough.
